study_type.value: Econometric study / case-control research letter: two-stage difference-in-differences regression with event-study framework, hospital-bed-weighted, comparing attacked, nearby-unattacked and unattacked hospitals

methodology.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
methodology.value: Authors constructed a database of US hospital ransomware attacks and linked it to 100% Medicare fee-for-service claims data; impacts on hospital operations and patient outcomes are quantified with event-study / continuous-treatment difference-in-differences estimators (Callaway-Goodman-Bacon-Sant'Anna style) around attack weeks. Record verified against Crossref DOI metadata (51 references) and the AEA abstract. JEL codes I12, I13, D83, K42.

methodology.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
methodology.value: Attacks identified from the HHS OCR breach portal cross-checked with online media coverage, restricted to attacks disruptive to care delivery. California hospital panel 2014-2020 (82,359,450 ED visits; 23,475,497 inpatient admissions): 8 disruptive ransomware attacks affecting 15 hospitals vs 355 unattacked hospitals, plus analysis of unattacked hospitals in the same hospital service area (n=17 nearby vs n=20 other). Two-stage difference-in-differences, bed-weighted, event-study specifications. Verified against the JAMA full text (PMC11137657) and PubMed.

key_findings.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
key_findings.value: Ransomware attacks reduce hospital volume by 17-24% during the initial attack week, with recovery within 3 weeks. Among patients already admitted when an attack begins, in-hospital mortality increases by 34-38%. These are among the first causal estimates directly tying hospital ransomware to excess deaths, quantifying the outcome justification for incident-response and cybersecurity investment in healthcare.

key_findings.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
key_findings.value: In attacked hospitals, weekly ED visits fell 8.10% (95% CI -14.40 to -1.80) in week 1 and 16.21% (95% CI -26.58 to -5.84) in week 2; inpatient admissions fell 8.16% (95% CI -19.92 to 3.60) in week 1 and 16.62% (95% CI -31.28 to -2.00) in week 2, returning to pre-attack levels within about 8 weeks. ED visits temporarily increased at unattacked nearby hospitals in the same service area, showing spillover displacement of care beyond targets.

limitations.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
limitations.value: Medicare claims cover predominantly elderly fee-for-service patients, limiting generalisation to younger/commercial populations; attack list depends on public reporting (underreporting of unreported attacks); attacks may be correlated with unobserved hospital characteristics, mitigated but not eliminated by identification strategy; short-run outcomes dominate the claims horizon.

limitations.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
limitations.value: Only 8 attacks/15 hospitals (small treatment count, wide CIs); single US state (California), 2014-2020 window predating the 2021-2023 attack surge; outcome restricted to ED visits and inpatient admissions (no clinical complication or mortality outcomes); attack identification relies on HHS portal plus media triangulation, possible mismeasurement. The research-letter format limits granularity.

research_gaps.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
research_gaps.value: Extends the literature from descriptive attack counts and ED-volume disruption to causal patient-outcome impacts (mortality); remaining gaps include non-Medicare populations, community/ambulatory clinics, cost-of-incident response, and mechanisms (e.g., delayed procedures) through which attacks raise mortality.

research_gaps.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
research_gaps.value: Identifies inter-hospital spillover effects as an under-measured dimension of ransomware harm; gaps remain in clinical outcomes of displaced patients (e.g., longer treatment times found in adjacent ED studies), multi-state replication, and post-2020 attack-wave evidence.

dataset_benchmark.value: Hospital ransomware-attack database constructed by the authors, linked to 100% Medicare FFS claims; replication data and code openly deposited at ICPSR (doi 10.3886/E235483V1, AEA publisher-hosted) - open-sourced (restricted-use Medicare data accessed through CMS/ResDAC channels)

dataset_benchmark.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
dataset_benchmark.value: HHS OCR breach portal attack list (gazetted publicly) combined with California statewide ED/inpatient data (82.4M ED visits, 23.5M admissions, 2014-2020); supplemental data-sharing statement available via JAMA; California OSHPD/state data are requestable, not fully open ([uncertain] whether analytic dataset is redistributed)

evaluation_metrics.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
evaluation_metrics.value: Health-outcome econometric metrics rather than ML metrics: percentage change in hospital volume during attack week (17-24% decrease), recovery time (3 weeks), and in-hospital mortality increase among admitted patients (34-38%) with confidence-interval-based inference; no F1/precision/recall or detection-latency metrics

evaluation_metrics.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
evaluation_metrics.value: Difference-in-differences percentage changes (95% CI) for weekly ED visits (-8.10% week 1, -16.21% week 2) and inpatient admissions (-8.16% / -16.62%), recovery horizon (~8 weeks), R-squared 0.90-0.98; no security-detection metrics

reproducibility.paper: Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients
reproducibility.value: High: AEA requires deposit of data and code - both publicly archived (ICPSR doi 10.3886/E235483V1); Medicare claims access requires CMS approval, but analysis recipes, event windows and identification strategy are externally auditable

reproducibility.paper: Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals
